Linear regression Wrap-up

Regression Example

Why do states target civilians in war?

  • Data from (Valentino, Huth, and Croco 2006)

Why do states target civilians in war?

  • Research Question: Why do some states engage in deliberate attacks on civilian populations during wartime? Why do some states refrain from doing this? Do international laws deter this kind of attack?
  • We see a great deal of variation in the number of civilians killed during war. Many wars see negligible deliberate civilian targeting, others see lots.

Why do states target civilians in war?

Some potential explanations:

  • International law/treaties: signing the Geneva Convention should decrease civilian targeting.

  • Regime type: democracies should be less likely to target civilians.

  • Racial or religious differences: civilian targeting will be more likely when the adversaries are mostly from different racial or religious groups.

  • Strategy: conflicts involving counter-insurgency, wars of attrition, with goals of conquest, or especially long lasting wars will see more civilian targeting.

Why do states target civilians in war?

  • Cases: all interstate wars from 1900 to 2003.

  • Unit of analysis: each observation represents a “side” in a single conflict (so one row for the U.S. in Vietnam, and another row for Vietnam).

  • Dependent Variable: logged number of civilian fatalities committed by this side.

  • Independent Variables: treaty status, regime type, racial/religious differences, variables reflecting war strategy/goals and duration.

  • Additional controls: relative capabilities, population.

State targeting of civilians

State targeting of civilians

  • Model 3 tests an interaction with regime type and treaty status. Is the effect of treaty status significantly different for democracies?
  • Model 4 tests an interaction with regime type and strategy. Is the effect of an attrition/counter-insurgency strategy significantly different for democracies?

State targeting of civilians

Ultimately, the strategic explanations (and controls) appear to have the most support here.

Some requirements for regression to “work”

Some requirements for regression to “work”

  • Regression relies on a lot of assumptions, but some of these are more important than others.

  • You can’t necessarily “fix” all of these problems, but you should think about them and try to mitigate them.

Some requirements for regression to “work”

Instead of giving an exhaustive list, we’ll focus on some of the problems that are most likely to come up in your analyses for this class:

  1. Variables must vary.

  2. Things should be linear (even if we have to force them)

  3. No omitted variable bias.

1. Variables must vary

Variables must vary

  • Regression models asks “what happens to Y when X changes?”. At a minimum, that means both X and Y should change.
  • This seems obvious, but it can show up in unexpected ways, especially when we’re including multiple predictors in a model.

Variables must vary

For instance, the DV in this model is 2020 turnout, and I’ve included controls for Biden’s share of the two party vote and Trump’s share of the two party vote…

regC(vep20.turnout ~  biden2020 + trump2020, data=states)

So what happened here?

Variables must vary

  • Adding a control variable is akin to asking “what happens to Y when X changes, hold constant for Z?”

  • But if Z and X don’t vary independently of each other, then its not possible to estimate this. Once I control for Trump’s 2020 vote share, Biden’s 2020 vote share no longer varies:

Variables must vary

  • This problem is called “perfect multicollinearity”, and it makes a regression model intractable, which is why R automatically drops perfectly collinear variables.

  • Near-perfect collinearity (X almost perfectly predicts Z) can also be a problem, but usually this comes up when we include variables that are almost exact copies.

Variables must vary

  • When near-perfect multicollinearity does show up, it tends to result in inflated standard errors.

  • In general, this is only a problem with the independent variables are extremely closely correlated (>.90), and is less of a concern when sample sizes are large.

Variability

  • Avoid including redundant variables in a model.

  • In general, remember parsimony: all else equal, a model with just a few variables is probably better than a model with dozens.

  • Remember that multicollinearity isn’t necessarily a big problem outside of extreme cases.

2. Things should be linear

Linearity

Linear regression fits straight lines, but many relationships are non-linear.

Linearity

In practice, this is less of a problem than it might appear at first glance: we can make things linear by coding variables differently. For example:

  • If the effect of X on Y depends on values of Z, we can use an interaction term

  • If X has a positive effect at low values but a negative effect at high levels, we might include a quadratic term (x + x^2) in the model

  • Both of these could still be expressed as linear models by transforming variables.

Linearity

There’s clearly something more complicated than a linear relationship here:

That said, we can make this a linear relationship by squaring X:

Linearity in categorical variables

We’ll often treated ordered variables as if they’re actually numeric, but the effect of X on Y may not actually be linear in the population.

Ordinal variables as numbers

If we remove the “Other” category, we can convert partyid to a number and then treat it as an interval-level variable.

survey$numeric_pid <- as.numeric(survey$party_id)
survey$numeric_pid[which(survey$party_id == "Other")] <- NA
survey$numeric_pid[which(survey$party_id == "Not sure")] <- NA

crosstabC(survey$party_id, survey$numeric_pid)

Ordinal variables as numbers

We can use the numeric variable in a regression model without too much of a problem:

regC(trump_actions_1 ~ numeric_pid , data =survey)

Ordinal variables as numbers

  • A one unit increase in “party ID” is associated with a 1.187 unit increase in supporting Trump’s efforts to end DEI.

  • We know that the effect of moving from being a Democrat to being an independent isn’t strictly linear, but this does capture a rough average.

  • If a variable has 5 or more categories, this is probably fine! and it simplifies your interpretation.

Ordinal variables

What if we’re really skeptical that the effect is numeric?

We have two* options.

  • Option 1: make a dummy and compare 1 group vs. all the rest

  • Option 2: include all categories as dummy variables

  • Option 3: we can use polynomials (X, X^2, X^3…) similar to the way we use an interaction term. But this is usually more trouble than its worth.

Ordinal variables: Option 1

  • Creating a single dummy variable that equals 1 for one or more categories will give us an estimate of the effect of being in that category vs. being in any other category.

  • For instance: this gives us a comparison of anyone who described themselves as a Democrat vs. all other groups (Independents are lumped in with Republicans!)

survey$Democrat<-transformC(type = 'dummy', 
           x= party_id, 
           response = c("Strong Democrat", 
                        "Not very strong Democrat",
                        "Independent Democrat"),
           data = survey,
           confirm = FALSE
           )

regC(trump_actions_1 ~ Democrat, data = survey)

Ordinal variables: Option 2

  • Alternatively, we can just include party_id as is, which will result in the variable being treated as categorical.

  • This means we would interpret every coefficient as the effect of being in that category relative to being in the excluded category (here: Strong Dems)

  • This complicates interpretation and sacrifices statistical power (we’re more likely to find false negatives) but it doesn’t require as many assumptions about the relationship between X and Y.

regC(trump_actions_1 ~ party_id, data = survey)

Nominal variables

  • If our variables are nominal, then we obviously can’t treat them as numeric! But we can either make a single dummy variable and compare one group vs. the rest:
survey$white<-transformC(type = 'dummy', 
           x=race_eth_combined, 
           response = 'White, non-Hispanic',
           data = survey,
           confirm = FALSE
           )

regC(trump_actions_1 ~ white, data = survey)
  • or create multiple dummies.
regC(trump_actions_1 ~ race_eth_combined, data=survey)

Linearity

For simplicity’s sake:

  • it will usually make sense to just re-code ordinal variables as numbers.

  • if you have a nominal predictor, it might make sense to make a single dummy and compare one group vs. all other groups.

  • This tends to be “okay” in practice, but you should keep in mind you’re changing what you’re estimating and introducing new assumptions when you do these things. So you should be able to talk about those, and how they might matter.

3. The model must be correct

Correct models and bias

  • In order for regression to produce accurate, unbiased estimates of the effect of an independent variable on the dependent variable, we need to correctly account for all confounding variables.

  • (In observational data, this is really hard to get right. You’re not expected to do it in this class, but you should be aware of some of the limitations this imposes on how you interpret your results.)

Omitted variables

  • To correctly estimate the effect of X on Y, we need to account for all potential confounding variables.

  • Its actually okay if we don’t include everything that explains Y! We should be worried about cases where an omitted variable is correlated with X and Y.

Omitted variables

Using simulated data: the actual equation here is: \(Y = 3X + -3Z + \text{error}\)

What will happen if I use a regression model without controlling for Z? Will I get the correct estimate of the effect of X on Y?

Omitted variables

\(Y = 3X + -3Z + \text{error}\)

Yes (within a small rounding error!)

Omitted variables

  • As long as the omitted variable in independent of X, we can estimate the effect of X without bias. “Z” just causes random noise around the regression line.

  • Our estimate of X becomes biased only when Z is correlated with X and we fail to account for it.

Omitted variables

When Z is correlated with X, we’re no longer able to estimate the effect of X correctly unless we control for Z

Omitted variables

  • % Catholic appears to matter for the percentage of people who smoke in a state

  • But this is probably spurious: cigarette taxes are correlated with both % Catholic and with % smokers, so controlling for this confounding makes the original relationship insignificant.

Omitted variables

  • A key difficulty here: we can’t control for everything! We can never have more predictors than observations, and models usually start to produce meaningless results well before that point.

  • This is why it’s hard to show causal relationships with observational research.

Bad controls

  • It’s also possible for the inclusion of some controls to introduce bias rather than alleviate it. One way this can happen is when controlling for something that is actually a consequence of the independent or dependent variable.

  • A classic example would be estimating the effects of education on earnings, while trying to control for “occupation”.

Bad controls

  • If occupation is caused by education, then controlling for occupation partial out some of the benefits of education.
  • In the extreme case, education might only influence earnings through its effect on occupation, in which case controlling for occupation would lead you to think education provided zero benefits.

Finding the right model

  • If you care about identifying cause-and-effect, you should try to control for things that are potential confounders: things that you think might cause both the IV and the DV.

  • You should avoid controlling for things that are caused by the IV and/or the DV.

  • This is always going to be really difficult in observational research.

4. Other issues

  • These are less important for your final paper but the book discusses them in some detail, so I’m including a little information on them here.

  • These are mostly surmountable problems.

Heteroskedasticity

  • OLS assumes that the error term \(\epsilon\) has a constant variance across levels of the independent variables (homoskedasticity)

  • In some cases, however, the variance in the error term might increase or decrease as the IVs increase in value.

Heteroskedasticity

The residuals from this model are pretty constant as we move from higher to lower expected values of Y

But in this case, we see heteroscedasticity: the variance changes as the expected value of Y gets big.

Heteroskedasticity

  • Data: Current Population Survey 2007

  • DV: Hourly Earnings

  • IV: Years of Education

  • We can see that the residual from the regression is increasing as the fitted values increase.

Heteroskedasticity

  • Heteroskedasticity can artificially deflate standard errors. So the biggest concern are false positives.

  • It can also be a sign of other issues: such as omitted variable bias or non-linear relationships.

  • Fortunately, we have a number of strategies for estimating standard errors that are “robust” to this kind of problem.

Autocorrelation

  • Observations are assumed to be independent from one another.

  • But this assumption is often violated. For instance, if we have time-series data on democracy for a single country, the value at year 1 is not independent of the value at year 2.

  • Lack of independence can cause false positives: we actually have very few truly independent observations here, so a regression model using this data would overstate our level of confidence in the results and shrink the standard error.

Autocorrelation

  • As with heteroskedasticity, there are ways to adjust standard errors to account for the lack of independence between individual observations.

  • Time trends can also be a source of omitted variable bias, and so time series models will often attempt to “control” for the effect of time.

Outliers

What is a regression outlier?

  • Outliers are conditionally unusual observations: not just high values of Y or X but higher than expected values of Y given X

  • Related to problems with skew, but you can have skew without outliers and vice versa

  • We’re usually most concerned about their potential to unduly influence results.

Conditional unusualness

  • Data: Varieties of Democracy (V-DEM)
  • DV: Liberal-Democracy Score in most recent year available
  • IV: per-capita GDP in the same year

Red is the original model, black is the model after excluding the two observations highlighted in red

What’s going on here? Does it make sense to drop these observations?

Cook’s Distance

How big is the problem?

One way to quantify an outlier is to calculate the effect of dropping an observation on the results. Cooks D for observation i is:

\[D_i = \frac{\sum^n_{j=1}(\hat{Y_j} - \hat{Y_{j(i)}})^2}{MSE}\]

  • \(\hat{Y_j}\) the prediction for observation j from the full regression

  • \(\hat{Y_{j(i)}}\) the prediction for observation j after eliminating observation i

  • \(MSE\) the mean squared error of the regression

So, higher values mean that observation i is exerting more influence on our results.

A rule of thumb suggests examining outliers that have a D value over \(4/n\) where \(n\) is the number of observations

Cook’s Distance

So what should be done here?

Don’t just drop stuff! First consider:

  • Check for errors. (if some joker told a survey taker they were 120 years old, then you can probably justify dropping them, but then you might want to check for other bad responses)

  • Consider transforming variables. For continuous positive numbers, the natural log can make things far more normal

  • Model it. Especially if you can come up with a systematic explanation for why certain observations are weird.

So what should be done here?

Here’s the result after logging GDP and including a control variable for logged oil revenues

Next up: Logistic regression

  • What if our outcome variable is dichotomous (voting/not-voting, war/no war, etc.)

  • Linear regressions can sort of work, but they can give nonsensical results and fit the data poorly.

  • Logistic regression allows us to realistically model dichotomous outcomes using a linear modeling framework.
